cards.claim: Detecting eye blinks is a challenging problem used for facial analysis tasks like deep fake detection and driver drowsiness monitoring.
cards.evidence_quote: Detecting eye blinks is a challenging problem that can be used to solve a number of facial analysis tasks; it can reveal deep fake manipulation, detect driver drowsiness, measure the level of attention and eye fatigue during task performance, and health disorders, among others.

cards.claim: Most existing approaches rely on face recognition and frame-wise classification, which struggle with short blinks or noisy data.
cards.evidence_quote: Most approaches depend on face recognition and frame-wise eye state classiﬁcation, even with the rise of transformer-based sequence models in many other research areas. However, these methods may struggle to handle cases where blinks occur for only a few frames or where input data are noisy or incomplete.

cards.claim: The paper categorizes blinking detection methods into feature-based, appearance-based, and motion-based approaches.
cards.evidence_quote: Three categories emerged in the last decade: (i) feature-based methods use predetermined higher-level features like iris and eye landmark distances, (ii) appearance-based methods utilize low-level eye representations (e.g., RGB texture) and then adopt learning algorithms to classify eye states, and (iii) motion-based methods use input representations that encode motion information or a sequence of eye-related features to determine eye states.

cards.claim: Feature-based methods use predetermined features like iris landmarks and aspect ratios to identify blink events.
cards.evidence_quote: (i) feature-based methods use predetermined higher-level features like iris and eye landmark distances

cards.claim: The authors propose BlinkLinMulT, a fast transformer-based framework for eye blink detection that combines low- and high-level feature sequences.
cards.evidence_quote: In this work, we propose a fast transformer-based framework for eye blink detection that can effectively combine low- and high-level feature sequences considering several challenges

cards.claim: BlinkLinMulT is a modified multi-modal transformer with linear attention that considers multiple inputs including RGB texture, landmarks, and head pose angles.
cards.evidence_quote: We present a modiﬁed multi-modal transformer with linear attention (LinMulT) [21], which considers multiple inputs, such as RGB texture, iris and eye landmarks, ear, and head pose angles.

cards.claim: The proposed approach is evaluated on blink presence detection and eye state recognition tasks using multiple public benchmark datasets.
cards.evidence_quote: The proposed approach is evaluated on blink presence detection and eye state recognition tasks and multiple public benchmark datasets.

cards.claim: Cross-dataset evaluations show that a single network trained on a union of datasets improves results compared to training on datasets separately.
cards.evidence_quote: Cross-dataset evaluations are performed to quantify the robustness of BlinkLinMulT on unseen samples and it is found that a single network trained on a union of datasets improves the results obtained on all datasets separately.

cards.claim: The authors propose BlinkLinMulT, a multimodal transformer for blink detection that replaces quadratic attention with linear versions to improve training efficiency.
cards.evidence_quote: We propose a fast multimodal transformer, called BlinkLinMulT... we replaced the quadratic attention modules with linear versions [28], providing similar performance [21] while being easier to train.

cards.claim: The proposed method uses cross-modal transformers to translate between landmark features and RGB texture embeddings.
cards.evidence_quote: Cross-modal transformers translate one information source (e.g., β, here associated with the landmark features) to another one (e.g., α, here associated with the RGB texture)

cards.claim: The system determines blink presence by applying a sigmoid to the maximum logit within the sequence.
cards.evidence_quote: by only considering the maximum of the logits within the sequence, a sigmoid is applied to determine whether blinking is present in the sequence

cards.claim: Eye patches are extracted and resized to 64x64 pixels for processing.
cards.evidence_quote: The eye patches are extracted and resized to 64 × 64 pixels.

cards.claim: The proposed BlinkLinMulT method uses a linear multimodal transformer to estimate blinks for each eye independently based on features from a backbone CNN.
cards.evidence_quote: These sets of features are utilized as inputs to a linear multimodal transformer that estimates blinks for each eye independently.

cards.claim: The system calculates final blink presence scores by averaging network logits and applying a sigmoid function.
cards.evidence_quote: The network logits are averaged, and a sigmoid function is applied to make a final decision to obtain the final blink presence score for the sequence

cards.claim: A backbone CNN is used to extract deep hidden representations of RGB eye patches.
cards.evidence_quote: Furthermore, a backbone CNN extracts deep hidden representations of the RGB eye patches.

cards.claim: The study evaluates the proposed architectures on four image datasets and five video datasets.
cards.evidence_quote: The architectures detailed in Section 2.2 have been trained and evaluated on four image datasets and five video datasets, as detailed next in Sections 3.1 and 3.2.

cards.claim: The CEW dataset lacks pre-defined training and test splits, requiring the use of a 10-fold cross-validation scheme to measure performance.
cards.evidence_quote: The CEW dataset does not have pre-deﬁned training and test images; therefore, similar to others in the literature, we employed a 10-fold cross-validation (CV) scheme to measure the performance of backbone models.

cards.claim: The MRL Eye dataset contains 84,898 infrared images captured under various lighting conditions and reflection modes.
cards.evidence_quote: This dataset contains 84,898 infrared images in low and high resolution captured by different sensors like RealSense, IDS, and Aptina. The images are captured in various lighting conditions (the annotations are “bad” and “good”) and under three reﬂection modes based on the size of reﬂections

cards.claim: The EyeBlink8 dataset consists of eight videos with 408 eye blinks annotated across 70,992 frames.
cards.evidence_quote: There are 408 eye blinks on 70,992 annotated frames with a resolution of 640 × 480.

cards.claim: The proposed BlinkLinMulT method was evaluated using F1 score as the main metric due to unbalanced class distributions in the datasets.
cards.evidence_quote: Due to the unbalanced nature of the datasets, we chose the F1 score as the main performance metric; however, precision (P), recall (R), and average precision (AP) are also calculated.

cards.claim: ResNet50 achieved the highest F1 score of 0.912 on the RT-BENEimg dataset, outperforming other backbones by a considerable margin.
cards.evidence_quote: DenseNet121 performed well with 0.883, but ResNet50 outperformed the other models by a considerable margin with a 0.912 F1 score and 0.946 AP.

cards.claim: Training on larger 224x224 images resulted in lower performance metrics compared to the 64x64 counterpart for ResNet50.
cards.evidence_quote: The CNN trained on the 224 × 224 images achieved lower performance metric scores in every case versus its 64 × 64 counterpart: 0.929 vs. 0.932 precision, 0.837 vs. 0.893 recall, 0.881 vs. 0.912 F1 score, and 0.918 vs. 0.946 AP.

cards.claim: Cross-dataset evaluation showed massive performance degradation when models trained on ZJU were evaluated on other datasets.
cards.evidence_quote: the same network can only achieve 0.652 on the CEW and 0.502 on the RT-BENEimg, showing a massive performance degradation, 30%, and 46%, respectively.

cards.claim: Training on the union of multiple datasets improved F1 scores across CEW, ZJU, and RT-BENEimg.
cards.evidence_quote: Training on the union of the datasets improved on previous results measured in Section 4.2: the F1 scores changed from 0.995 to 0.997 on CEW, from 0.927 to 0.933 on ZJU, and from 0.883 to 0.913 RT-BENEimg.

cards.claim: The BlinkLinMulT model achieved high accuracy in eye state recognition and blink presence detection on the RT-BENEseq dataset.
cards.evidence_quote: The proposed BlinkLinMulT predicts frame-wise eye state scores, which are also used for determining the position of the blink event within the sequence, and then the blink presence is determined and results for both tasks are reported in Table 4.

cards.claim: The BlinkLinMulT model achieved perfect detection performance on the RN30 dataset during cross-dataset evaluation.
Performance degradation occurred when the network was not fine-tuned using MRL images.
cards.evidence_quote: We observed a 3.8% degradation if we are not ﬁne-tuning the network using the MRL images, and also the F1 score is increased by 2% if the MRL train set is added to the union of the training databases.

cards.claim: Training on a union of multiple datasets improved eye state recognition F1 scores across EyeBlink8, RN15, and RN30 benchmarks.
cards.evidence_quote: Table 6 shows that the eye state recognition and blink presence detection performance are consistently improved compared to those experiments, where only a single dataset is used for training. BlinkLinMulT captured the unique patterns from all used datasets; therefore, the eye state recognition F1 score increased from 0.723 to 0.87 for EyeBlink8, 0.792 to 0.871 for RN15, and 0.792 to 0.836 for RN30.

cards.claim: The proposed BlinkLinMulT model achieved superior blink presence detection performance compared to state-of-the-art methods on the TalkingFace dataset.
cards.evidence_quote: The proposed BlinkLinMulT excels in the blink presence detection task on all datasets. ... Ours 1.000 1.000 1.000

cards.claim: Combining texture with iris and face mesh landmarks improved performance over using texture alone on the RT-BENEimg dataset.
cards.evidence_quote: While the iris and eye landmark features alone show fairly low performance, combining them with the texture further improves the performance on RT-BENEimg compared to texture-only evaluation (0.922 vs. 0.913 F1 scores).

cards.claim: The network's per-frame eye state recognition metrics are slightly lower due to frame-shifting during decoding and annotation boundaries starting or ending with an open eye.
cards.evidence_quote: The per-frame evaluation metrics of the eye state recognition task are slightly lower; however, this is due to occasional frame-shifting during decoding and the fact that annotation often starts and ends with an open eye.

cards.claim: The BlinkLinMulT model achieves a perfect 1.0 F1 score on the TalkingFace dataset for blink presence detection.
cards.evidence_quote: in the last case, where all feature sequences are used, the problematic extreme blinks when the person looks down are detected in TalkingFace, achieving a 1.0 F1 score in the blink presence detection task.

cards.claim: Transformer-based sequence modeling outperforms frame-wise estimations for blink detection.
cards.evidence_quote: In Table 9, the transformer-based sequence modeling shows superiority over frame-wise estimations.

cards.claim: Model performance drops at high yaw angles due to self-occlusion and imbalanced class distribution.
cards.evidence_quote: The result of the experiment revealed that the performance of the model drops at higher yaw angles compared to the frontal faces; the 0.917 F1 score is calculated from 633 blink samples for >25◦angles compared to the 0.951 average F1 score from 10,962 frontal samples.

cards.claim: Extreme head pose angles, particularly positive pitch where participants look down, cause most errors due to eyelid visibility and landmark precision issues.
cards.evidence_quote: Most of the errors originated from this extreme head pose because the eyelids are more visible, they move over a shorter distance, and the landmark-based features are less precise considering the available resolution.

cards.claim: The proposed BlinkLinMulT model achieves comparable or superior performance to state-of-the-art models on blink detection and eye state recognition tasks.
cards.evidence_quote: Our results demonstrate comparable or superior performance compared to state-of-the-art models on blink presence detection and eye state recognition tasks, using public benchmark databases.

cards.claim: The authors propose BlinkLinMulT, a transformer-based model that efficiently combines low- and high-level features from video sequences using linear complexity attention mechanisms.
cards.evidence_quote: We propose BlinkLinMulT, a novel transformer-based blink detection model that efﬁciently combines low- and high-level features from video sequences using linear complexity attention mechanisms.

cards.claim: The paper demonstrates that training a single network on a union of datasets improves results across all individual datasets, assessing robustness on unseen samples.
cards.evidence_quote: We performed cross-dataset evaluations to assess the robustness of BlinkLinMulT on unseen samples, demonstrating that a single network trained on a union of datasets improves results across all datasets individually.

cards.claim: The study shows that increased eye patch dimensionality of low-resolution patches degrades the performance of current SOTA backbones like CLIP ViT-B/16.
cards.evidence_quote: We showed how increased eye patch dimensionality of low-resolution eye patches degrades the performance of current SOTA backbones, e.g., CLIP ViT-B/16 dependence

cards.claim: The BlinkLinMulT model achieves high accuracy across different head orientations, with F1 scores above 0.95 for most yaw and pitch angles.
cards.evidence_quote: Table A4. Blink presence prediction performance of the proposed BlinkLinMulT. Test samples from all 5 sequence datasets are used for the experiment. Yaw and pitch degrees are predicted by 3DDFA_V2. Extreme yaw and pitch angles, when the participant is looking sideways or down, might cause slightly decreased performance.

cards.claim: Performance decreases slightly when participants look sideways or down due to extreme yaw and pitch angles.
cards.evidence_quote: Extreme yaw and pitch angles, when the participant is looking sideways or down, might cause slightly decreased performance.

cards.claim: The DenseNet121 backbone achieves the highest F1 score of 0.995 on the CEW dataset within-dataset evaluation.
The DenseNet121 backbone trained on the union of datasets achieves an F1 score of 0.851 when tested on the ZJU dataset.
